div.p: Background Meningiomas are common central nervous system tumors with few available treatment choices. This research investigates the role of LTBP2 in meningioma biology, emphasizing its ability to be a therapeutic goal.

Methods Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were recognized from the GSE84263 dataset. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) revealed correlated gene modules. Hub genes were discovered via an analysis of the proteinprotein interaction (PPI) network, with LTBP2 selected for further study. LTBP2 expression was analyzed utilizing Western blotting (WB) and quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction in normal human meningeal cells (NHMCs) and meningioma cell lines. Functional assays assessed cell invasion and migration, proliferation, and apoptosis. Glycolysis was assessed through glucose uptake, lactate production, and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurements. WB analysis assessed related protein levels in the PI3K/AKT and mTOR/c-Myc pathways in meningioma cells.

div.head: Results
div.p: The analysis identified 492 upregulated and 677 downregulated genes, with the green module significantly correlated. Six overlapping genes showed elevated expression in tumors. LTBP2 was upregulated in meningioma cells. Functional assays showed that LTBP2 knockdown reduced proliferation, invasion, and migration while increasing apoptosis, whereas its overexpression had the opposite effect, enhancing aggressive cellular behaviors. LTBP2 also promoted glycolysis, as shown by increased lactate production, glucose uptake and ECAR, along with decreasd OCR. Mechanistic studies revealed that LTBP2 activated the PI3K/AKT and mTOR/c-Myc signaling pathways, with c-Myc mediating the glycolytic effects of LTBP2. Importantly, c-Myc knockdown reversed the impacts of LTBP2 on cell invasion, proliferation, and apoptosis. Conclusion LTBP2 plays a critical role in meningioma progression by activating the PI3K/AKT and mTOR/c-Myc signaling pathways, highlighting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Meningiomas are the predominant primary tumor in the central nervous system, typically considered benign and slow-growing [1]. However, they exhibit a wide range of biological behaviors-including differences in growth rate, invasiveness, and recurrence potential-that correlate with the World Health Organization (WHO) classification into grades 1, 2, and 3. Higher grades meningiomas are more likely to exhibit aggressive and invasive characteristics [2]. In recent decades, the incidence of meningiomas has steadily increased, especially in individuals over 40, with risk rising significantly with age [3]. Meningiomas are also more prevalent in females, with an incidence substantially higher than in males, typically ranging from 1.5 to 2 times greater, likely influenced by hormonal factors such as estrogen and progesterone [4]. e mainstay of treatment is still surgical resection, which aims to remove the tumor as much as possible while maintaining neurological function [5]. Despite favorable outcomes in low-grade meningiomas, recurrence remains a persistent obstacle to effective long-term disease control-particularly in higher-grade tumors or those deemed surgically inaccessible due to their location near critical neurovascular structures, which limits the feasibility of complete resection [6,7]. ese clinical variations are closely associated with distinct biological and molecular features, as reflected in the WHO classification system, which incorporates both histological and genetic criteria. As such, more effective treatment approaches need a knowledge of the underlying molecular pathways guiding meningioma progression.

Latent transforming growth factor-β binding protein 2 (LTBP2), a member of the latent TGF-β binding protein family, plays a critical function in regulating the activation of TGF-β [8]. While LTBP2 is essential for normal tissue homeostasis, accumulating evidence indicates that it is also implicated in tumorigenesis. For instance, Zhang Y et al. demonstrated that LTBP2 is highly expressed in gliomas, and its knockdown suppresses tumor growth and migration by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt/mTOR cascade [9]. Similarly, Wang J et al. reported that the circEPSTI1/miR-942-5p/LTBP2 axis promotes invasion and proliferation by in oral squamous carcinoma by facilitating epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and activating the PI3K/Akt/mTOR cascade [10].

Cancer cells frequently reprogram their metabolism to support rapid proliferation, with enhanced glycolysis (even under normoxic conditions) being a hallmark of many malignancies. Notably, the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/c-Myc signaling cascade is not only a key regulator of oncogenic signaling but also plays a central role in cancer metabolism, particularly glycolysis-a hallmark of malignant transformation. In pancreatic cancer and leukemia, for instance, the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/c-Myc signaling cascade has been shown to regulate the glycolytic pathway, thereby contributing to tumor metabolic reprogramming [11,12]. Akt activation enhances glycolysis by upregulating key glycolytic enzymes, thereby providing tumor cells with increased energy and biosynthetic intermediates for rapid proliferation [13,14]. Additionally, c-Myc promotes glycolytic flux by transcriptionally activating genes involved in glucose uptake and lactate production. For example, Tang H et al. demonstrated that PDGFRβ promotes glycolysis by activating the PI3K/ Akt/mTOR/c-Myc pathway in osteosarcoma cells [15]. Among the six hub genes identified in our bioinformatics analysis-BMP4, CDH1, FMOD, LTBP2, SFRP2, and TGFB2-LTBP2 was chosen for further investigation because it remains largely unexplored in the context of meningiomas. While other candidates such as CDH1 and TGFB2 have been previously implicated in tumor invasion and TGF-β signaling, LTBP2 stands out due to its dual role in extracellular matrix organization and modulation of intracellular signaling pathways, particularly the PI3K/AKT cascade. However, its functional relevance in meningiomas remains largely unexplored, making it a promising target for further investigation in the context of tumor progression. is knowledge gap presented an opportunity for novel discovery. Given the involvement of LTBP2 in tumor progression in other cancers such as gliomas [16], further investigation into its function in meningiomas may help elucidate potential molecular mechanisms and identify candidate targets for future therapeutic exploration.

Although the involvement of LTBP2 in tumor progression has been described in other cancer types, its role in meningiomas has not been elucidated, making this study the first to characterize LTBP2's oncogenic and metabolic functions in this tumor type. Meningiomas are the most common primary tumors of the central nervous system, and despite generally favorable outcomes for benign forms, higher-grade and recurrent tumors still present significant clinical challenges. Importantly, the metabolic landscape of meningiomas is increasingly recognized as a potential therapeutic target, yet the upstream regulators of glycolytic reprogramming in these tumors are not fully defined. e PI3K/ AKT/mTOR pathway is frequently activated in meningiomas due to upstream genetic alterations such as NF2 loss [17], and has been associated with enhanced proliferation and resistance to apoptosis in high-grade tumors.

Given the established role of LTBP2 in modulating the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway and the central importance of glycolysis in tumor progression, we hypothesized that LTBP2 may contribute to meningioma malignancy through regulation of glycolytic metabolism.

erefore, our research aimed to investigate the role of LTBP2 in regulating glycolytic metabolism and key tumorigenic behaviors such as proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis in meningioma cells. Understanding these mechanisms may support the development of targeted therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes.

div.head: Gene expression data retrieval and differential expression analysis
div.p: In this study, we utilized the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO, h t t p s : / / w w w . n c b i . n l m . n i h . g o v / g d s / ) database to select the GSE84263 dataset, which comprises 96 mutated meningioma samples and 25 normal samples. e "Limma" program in R software was employed to do differential expression analysis of the genes in the GSE84263 dataset. Genes were filtered based on the criteria of fold change (FC), with an FC > 2 indicating upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and an FC < 0.5 indicating downregulated DEGs. P < 0.05 has been the significance level to assess statistical significance, allowing the recognition of relevant DEGs linked to meningioma pathology.

div.head: Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA)
div.p: To examine the co-expression relationships among differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with meningioma, we performed WGCNA. DEGs were identified from the GSE84263 dataset by fold change (FC) and P-value thresholds. e co-expression network involving these DEGs was established utilizing the Bioinfo Intelligent Cloud platform (https://www.bic.ac.cn/BIC/#/). For scale-free topology, an ideal soft-thresholding power of 16 was chosen.

is framework clustered genes into distinct co-expression modules, each symbolized by a different color for clear identification. e module eigengenes were calculated, and their correlations with clinical traits (tumor and normal samples) were assessed. Modules with high correlation were selected for further analysis.

div.head: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis and candidate genes identification
div.p: After identifying the significantly associated modules, the genes within these modules were subjected by the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes (STRING) database (https://string-db.org/) to PPI network analysis. To identify the top ten genes, we used three ranking methods: maximum clique centrality (MCC), Degree of Maximal Network Connectivity (DMNC), and edge permeation component (EPC) through the cytoHubba plugin of the Cytoscape program. Subsequently, the Venn online graphical tool ( h t t p s : / / b i o i n f o r m a t i c s . p s b . u g e n t . b e / w e b t o o l s / V e n n /) was applied to analyze the overlap between genes identified by the three algorithms. To confirm the expression of these overlapping genes further, their expression levels in tumor and normal samples were evaluated using the Sangerbox platform (3.0, h t t p : / / v i p . s a n g e r b o x . c o m / h o m e . h t m l ) , and box plots were generated for visualization.

div.head: Cell culture
div.p: Meningioma cell lines (CH157-MN, IOMM-Lee, and Ben-Men-1) and normal Human Mesangial Cells (HMCs) were purchased from BioVector NTCC (Beijing, China). All cell types were cultivated in DMEM and added with 1% penicillin-streptomycin and 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). At 37 °C, the cells were cultivated with 5% CO 2 in a humidified incubator to ensure optimal growth conditions.

div.head: Cell transfection and treatment
div.p: Ben-Men-1 and IOMM-Lee cells were planted at a density of 2 × 10 cells per well in 24-well plates and cultivated in a complete medium for the whole night until reaching 70-80% confluence. In accordance with the manufacturer's guidelines, transfection was performed utilizing Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, Shanghai, China). Meningioma cells were transfected with either siRNAs targeting LTBP2 (si-LTBP2) or negative control siRNA (si-NC), and plasmids for LTBP2 overexpression (over-LTBP2) or a control vector (over-NC). In a separate set of experiments, siRNAs targeting c-Myc (si-c-Myc) or si-NC were introduced into cells already transfected with over-LTBP2. Cells were harvested for further experiments after 48 h of transfection. To assess the effects of si-LTBP2 and SC79 (an AKT activator), cells subjected to si-LTBP2 transfection were exposed to 10 µM SC79 or DMSO for 24 h before further analysis.

div.head: Quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR)
div.p: TRIzol reagent (Tiangen, China) was applied to separate total RNA from cultivated cells in compliance with the manufacturer's instructions. To synthesize complementary DNA (cDNA), the PrimeScript RT reagent kit (Takara, China) was utilized. Gene expression levels were determined by qRT-PCR utilizing SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China) on a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Wcgene Biotech, Inc., Shanghai, China). GAPDH served as the internal control for normalization. e 2 -ΔΔCt technique was applied to evaluate the relative levels. Table 1 lists the primers utilized in the qRT-PCR.

div.head: Western blotting (WB)
div.p: Protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Selleck, Shanghai, China) were added to the RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, China) to facilitate the extraction of proteins from cells. Quantification of protein concentrations was performed utilizing a BCA protein assay kit from Beyotime (China). Protein was applied to a PVDF membrane after being divided into equal portions employing SDS-PAGE (Beyotime, China). After that, the membranes were treated with primary antibodies particular for LTBP2 (1:1000), HK2 (1:5000), GLUT1 (1:1000), PKM2 (1:10000), LDHA (1:1000), PI3K (1:5000), p-PI3K (1:1000), p-AKT (1:1000), AKT (1:500), mTOR (1:5000), p-mTOR (1:2000), c-Myc (1:1000), and GAPDH (1:5000) as a loading control. All antibodies were sourced from abcam, Cambridge, UK. After incubating with suitable secondary antibodies, protein bands were detected utilizing ECL detection reagents (Tanon, Shanghai, China) and captured using a ChemiDoc imaging system.

div.head: Transwell assays for cell migration and invasion
div.p: Cell migration and invasion were evaluated utilizing a Transwell system (Biofavor, Shanghai, China). For the migration assay, 500 µL of full media including serum was subjected to the lower chamber, and 200 µL of a serum-free cell suspension was added to the top chamber. Following the incubation period, the membrane was stained with DAPI at room temperature for 15 min after the cells on the top surface were scraped with a cotton swab. Cell counts on the lower surface were tallied by an inverted microscope (×200) in five randomly chosen areas, and images were captured. e membrane was pre-coated with Matrigel (BD Biosciences, Shanghai, China) for the invasion experiment, and then the same protocol as for the migration assay was followed.

div.head: Flow cytometry analysis
div.p: e apoptosis rate of meningioma cells IOMM-Lee and Ben-Men-1 was evaluated using flow cytometry. After trypsinization and PBS washing, cells were incubated at room temperature with 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 5 µL of propidium iodide (PI) for 15 min. Subsequently, the staining was evaluated utilizing a flow cytometer (Guangzhou Jiyuan), and the results were assessed by quantifying the live cell population and the apoptotic

div.head: Glucose uptake and lactate production assays
div.p: Ben-Men-1 and IOMM-Lee cell lines were planted in an incubator with 5% CO 2 at 37 °C until reaching 70%-80% confluence, after which transfection and treatments were applied. Twenty-four hours post-treatment, centrifugation was used to gather the supernatant. Glucose uptake and lactate production were determined utilizing an assay kit for lactate and glucose (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China) to quantify, respectively, following the manufacturer's protocols. After normalizing the glucose uptake and lactate generation levels to cell counts, and statistical analysis was utilized to assess the results.

div.head: Seahorse extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) and oxygen consumption rate (OCR) assaysseahorse
div.p: e ECAR and OCR were measured using the Seahorse XF Glycolysis Stress Test Kit and the Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (Agilent Technologies, USA), respectively, according to the manufacturer's instructions. IOMM-Lee and Ben-Men-1 meningioma cells were seeded in Seahorse XF96 cell culture microplates at a density of 1 × 10 cells/ well and incubated overnight. For ECAR analysis, cells were sequentially treated with glucose (10 mM), oligomycin (1 µM), and 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG, 50 mM). For OCR analysis, cells were sequentially treated with oligomycin (1 µM), FCCP (1 µM), and a mixture of rotenone (0.5 µM) and antimycin A (0.5 µM). Measurements were taken using a Seahorse XF Analyzer (Agilent) and normalized to total protein content. Data were analyzed using Wave software (Agilent), and all assays were performed in triplicate.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: R software was employed for analysis, and all data was presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). A two-tailed Student's t-test was utilized to compare the two groups. A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Tukey's post-hoc test were utilized to compare groups with each other. e threshold for statistical significance was set at P-value < 0.05. Unless specified otherwise, every experiment was carried out in triplicate.

div.head: Identification of DEGs and construction of the co-expression network
div.p: DEGs were selected based on FC and P-value from the GSE84263 dataset. Among the identified DEGs, 677 were downregulated, and 492 were upregulated (Fig. 1A). ese DEGs were then subjected to WGCNA to explore their potential biological relevance.

As shown in Fig. 1B, an optimal soft-thresholding power of 16 was chosen to ensure a scale-free topology. To determine clusters of genes with high co-expression, WGCNA was applied to group these DEGs into distinct gene modules, each assigned a unique color (Fig. 1C). We examined eigengene correlations to understand the relationships between these modules further (Fig. 1D). e green module showed a significant correlation with the samples (correlation coefficient r = 0.799 and r = 0.779), indicating a strong association (Fig. 1E). is high correlation suggests that genes within the green module may have potential biological relevance based on the GSE84263 dataset.

div.head: Identification of candidate genes in the green module through PPI network analysis
div.p: To further explore the genes within the key green module, an analysis of PPI network was performed. ree algorithms, including MCC (10 nodes, 12 edges), DMNC (10 nodes, 13 edges), and EPC (10 nodes, 15 edges), were employed to identify the ten most interconnected genes (Fig. 2A and C). Subsequent topological analysis revealed six candidate genes: BMP4, CDH1, FMOD, LTBP2, SFRP2, and TGFB2 (Fig. 2D). To verify the relevance of such candidate genes, the GSE84263 dataset was used for expression validation in normal and tumor tissues. e levels of all six genes were noticeably greater in tumor tissues (Fig. 2E). Given the limited research on the association of LTBP2 with meningioma, this study selected LTBP2 as a hub gene for further study.

div.head: LTBP2 expression and transfection efficiency in human meningeal and meningioma cells
div.p: e expression of LTBP2 in HMCs and meningioma cell lines was analyzed by WB and qRT-PCR methods. e outcomes demonstrated that compared to HMCs, the levels of LTBP2 were significantly greater in lines of meningioma cells (Fig. 3A and C). Notably, the highest LTBP2 expression was observed in IOMM-Lee and Ben-Men-1 cells. erefore, these two cell lines were selected for subsequent functional experiments to investigate the biological role of LTBP2 in meningioma. To further validate the efficiency of LTBP2 knockdown and overexpression in meningioma cell lines, qRT-PCR and WB were performed after transfection with si-LTBP2 or over-LTBP2 plasmids. e knockdown of LTBP2 significantly reduced its expression, while overexpression resulted in a marked increase in LTBP2 levels (Fig. 3D and H).

div.head: Effects of LTBP2 knockdown and overexpression on meningioma cell phenotypes
div.p: Further research was applied to explore the impact of LTBP2 knockdown and overexpression on meningioma cell behavior. CCK-8 assays disclosed that meningioma cell proliferation was markedly inhibited by LTBP2 knockdown, whereas LTBP2 overexpression caused a discernible rise in cell proliferation (Fig. 4A and B). e subsequent research assessed the impacts of LTBP2 on cell invasion and migration. e findings demonstrated that LTBP2 knockdown significantly impaired both the capacity for migration and invasion of Ben-Men-1 and IOMM-Lee cells, while LTBP2 overexpression enhanced these capabilities (Fig. 4C and D). Finally, flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that LTBP2 knockdown promoted apoptosis in both cell lines, whereas LTBP2 overexpression suppressed apoptosis (Fig. 4E and F). ese findings indicate that LTBP2 promotes cell proliferation, enhances invasive and migratory abilities, and inhibits apoptosis in meningioma cells, suggesting its potential role in tumor progression.

div.head: LTBP2 knockdown and overexpression regulate glucose uptake, lactate production, and glycolysis-related protein expression in meningioma cells
div.p: Glucose uptake and lactate production were detected in IOMM-Lee and Ben-Men-1cells after LTBP2 knockdown or overexpression.

e outcomes established that the knockdown of LTBP2 markedly reduced glucose uptake and lactate generation, while (D and E) LTBP2 mRNA levels in Ben-Men-1 (D) and IOMM-Lee (E) cells after transfection with si-LTBP2, over-LTBP2, or their respective controls, measured by qRT-PCR (one-way ANOVA). (F-H) WB analysis of LTBP2 protein expression after transfection with si-LTBP2, over-LTBP2, or their respective controls in Ben-Men-1 (G) and IOMM-Lee (H) cells (one-way ANOVA). GAPDH was used as the loading control. qRT-PCR: Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction; WB: Western blotting. *P < 0.05 LTBP2 overexpression enhanced both processes (Fig. 5A and D). e levels of key markers related to glycolysis, such as LDHA, HK2, PKM2, and GLUT1, were examined.

LTBP2 knockdown resulted in a notable decline in the mRNA expression of these glycolysis genes in meningioma cells (Fig. 5E and G). In contrast, LTBP2 overexpression increased the expression of LDHA, PKM2, HK2, and GLUT1 mRNA in both cell lines (Fig. 5F and H). WB analysis also verified this outcome at the protein level (Fig. 5I and M). ese findings imply that LTBP2 enhances glycolysis by controlling the levels of key factors involved in glycolysis, thereby contributing to enhanced glucose metabolism in meningioma cells.

To further validate the role of LTBP2 in regulating glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration, we conducted Seahorse extracellular flux assays. e ECAR results revealed that LTBP2 knockdown significantly decreased glycolytic activity, while its overexpression markedly increased ECAR levels in both IOMM-Lee and Ben-Men-1 cells (Fig. 6A and B). Conversely, OCR analysis showed an opposite trend: knockdown of LTBP2 enhanced oxygen consumption, whereas its overexpression suppressed OCR (Fig. 6C and D).

ese results further support that LTBP2 promotes glycolysis and suppresses oxidative phosphorylation in meningioma cells. 3.6 LTBP2 activates the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway to regulate mTOR/c-Myc signaling pathway in meningioma cells e mTOR/c-Myc and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways form an interconnected network crucial for cell growth and metabolic regulation.

is study examined the effects of LTBP2 knockdown and combined treatment with SC79, an AKT activator, on the levels of pathway-related proteins in meningioma cells (Fig. 6E and H). WB analysis showed that LTBP2 knockdown markedly decreased the amounts of c-Myc, p-AKT, p-PI3K, and p-mTOR in both meningioma cell lines, while the expression of total PI3K, AKT, and mTOR did not alter considerably. To further confirm the function of the AKT pathway, cells were exposed to SC79 (the AKT activator). Rescue experiments demonstrated that the inhibitory impact of LTBP2 knockdown on the PI3K/AKT/mTOR/c-Myc cascade was reversed by activating AKT via SC79, as shown by PI3K, AKT, and mTOR phosphorylation expression, as well as the restoration of c-Myc expression.

div.head: c-Myc mediates the effect of LTBP2 on glycolysis in meningioma cells
div.p: Comparing meningioma cells to HMCs, qRT-PCR analysis revealed a substantial increase in c-Myc mRNA expression (Fig. 7A). To confirm successful c-Myc knockdown, qRT-PCR assays and WB assays were performed following transfection with c-Myc knockdown plasmids in IOMM-Lee cells and Ben-Men-1 cells, verifying efficient knockdown (Fig. 7B and D). Our previous experimental results showed that LTBP2 promoted glycolysis in meningioma cells. To explore the function of c-Myc in LTBP2-mediated glycolysis further, cells were treated with LTBP2 overexpression plasmids combined E-H) Glucose uptake and lactate production were measured in Ben-Men-1 (E, G) and IOMM-Lee (F, H) cells transfected with over-NC, over-LTBP2, over-LTBP2 + si-NC, or over-LTBP2 + si-c-Myc (one-way ANOVA). (I-M) qRT-PCR (I, J) and WB (K-M) analysis of glycolysis-related markers (LDHA, PKM2, HK2, and GLUT1) in Ben-Men-1 and IOMM-Lee cells after transfection with over-NC, over-LTBP2, over-LTBP2 + si-NC, or over-LTBP2 + si-c-Myc (one-way ANOVA). GAPDH was used as the internal control for qRT-PCR and the loading control for WB. qRT-PCR: Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction; WB: Western blotting. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 with c-Myc knockdown. Glucose uptake and lactate production assays showed that LTBP2 overexpression significantly increased glycolysis in contrast to the group under control. However, c-Myc knockdown effectively reversed these impacts, reducing both the absorption of glucose and the generation of lactate (Fig. 7E and H). Furthermore, qRT-PCR and WB analyses indicated that LTBP2 overexpression promoted the levels of glycolysis-related markers (LDHA, HK2, PKM2, and GLUT1), whereas the combination of LTBP2 overexpression and c-Myc knockdown greatly decreased the levels of protein and mRNA of these glycolysis-related proteins (Fig. 7I and M). ese results imply that LTBP2 regulates glycolysis in meningioma cells via mTOR/c-Myc signaling pathway activation in meningioma cells.

div.head: c-Myc knockdown reverses LTBP2-induced proliferation, invasion, migration, and apoptosis resistance in meningioma cells
div.p: To assess the importance of c-Myc in LTBP2-induced tumorigenic properties, we evaluated cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and apoptosis in two meningioma cell lines after c-Myc knockdown. LTBP2 overexpression markedly increased cell proliferation in meningioma cells by CCK-8 assays. However, knockdown of c-Myc effectively reversed this proliferative effect (Fig. 8A and B). e invasion and migration of cells were assessed via Transwell assays. e outcomes showed that LTBP2 overexpression enhanced both migration and invasion capabilities in two meningioma cell lines. Notably, c-Myc knockdown significantly suppressed these LTBP2-induced enhancements (Fig. 8C and D). Flow cytometry analysis demonstrated that LTBP2 overexpression decreased apoptosis rates in both cell lines. Conversely, c-Myc knockdown restored apoptosis levels, indicating a critical role for c-Myc in LTBP2-mediated regulation of meningioma cell phenotypes (Fig. 8E and F).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumors, making it essential to understand their etiology and molecular characteristics for advancing treatment strategies [18]. With the progress of molecular biology, targeted therapies for meningiomas are emerging, setting the stage for personalized medicine. Pawloski JA et al. extensively reviewed the genetic mutations in meningiomas, highlighting their impact on tumor grade, location, and the potential for genomic-targeted therapies [19]. Chen WC et al. identified a 36-gene prognostic signature capable of predicting postoperative recurrence risk, emphasizing the need for molecular biomarkers in meningioma management [20]. In this study, we employed bioinformatics approaches, including differential expression analysis, WGCNA, and PPI network analysis, to determine the six essential genes connected to meningiomas. Notably, Zhou Y et al. reported BMP4 to be significantly upregulated in IDH-mutant gliomas, suggesting its role in promoting tumor migration and invasion [21]. CDH1, a gene involved in the EMT, also demonstrates clinical significance in meningiomas [22]. e SFRP2 gene was also identified as one of the new predictors of brain tumors, suggesting its potential importance in distinguishing brain tumor subtypes such as meningioma and glioblastoma [23]. Although FMOD has been implicated in tumor progression and extracellular matrix remodeling in several cancers, such as breast and colorectal cancer [24,25], its role in meningiomas remains largely unexplored.

is makes FMOD a potential candidate for future studies investigating its relevance in meningioma pathogenesis. TGFB2 serves as a critical activator in the TGF-β signaling pathway, regulating cell proliferation and differentiation. Fu XH et al. indicated that exosomes derived from M2 polarized macrophages (M2-MDEs) are enriched in meningioma tissues, facilitating tumor cell migration, proliferation, and oncogenesis by activating the TGF-β cascade [26]. Given the limited research on LTBP2 in meningiomas, our research attempts to investigate its function in the development of tumors and its interaction with key molecular pathways. In our study, LTBP2 was discovered upregulated in meningioma cells compared to normal human meningeal cells. In vitro cell experiments demonstrated that LTBP2 knockdown suppressed the invasion, proliferation, and migration of meningioma cells while promoting apoptosis. Conversely, LTBP2 overexpression increased cell invasion, migration, and proliferation, and reduced apoptosis, suggesting that LTBP2 may contribute to the malignant behavior of meningiomas by fostering tumor growth and metastatic potential. ese findings align with previous research on LTBP2 in various cancers. For instance, Zhou C et al. reported that LTBP2 knockdown in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) reduced proliferation and promoted vascular remodeling, highlighting its role in cell growth regulation [27]. Additionally, LTBP2 was shown to regulate apoptosis in intracranial aneurysm models, where its knockdown inhibited apoptosis, further supporting the pro-survival role of LTBP2 in disease pathology. Furthermore, Zhao J et al. analyzed eleven papers in a meta-analysis, establishing LTBP2 as a significant prognostic factor in malignant tumors, with high expression levels correlating with poorer survival outcomes [28]. Interestingly, Zhang X et al. reported that LTBP2 was downregulated in prostate cancer cells, where its suppression of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway resulted in reduced metastasis and proliferation [29]. When all findings are combined, they indicate that LTBP2 may play distinct roles in different tumor types, potentially depending on the context of its expression and interaction with signaling pathways.

Recent studies have showed the strong link between meningioma metabolism and glycolysis, the process of converting glucose into lactate, often enhanced in hypoxic conditions [30]. Glycolysis plays a key role in cancer, with markers like HK2, GLUT1, PKM2, and LDHA serving critical functions [31]. HK2 initiates the glycolytic process, GLUT1 facilitates glucose uptake, PKM2 regulates the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, and LDHA converts pyruvate to lactate, one of the main characteristics of the Warburg effect in cancers [32]. Yadav D et al. linked GLUT1 and HK2 overexpression to more aggressive tumor behavior, suggesting that targeting these enzymes could enhance cancer treatments [33]. Additionally, Cheng H et al. showed that modulating glycolysis through the CBX7/USP44/c-MYC/LDHA axis could inhibit meningioma proliferation, indicating that targeting metabolic pathways may offer therapeutic advantages [34]. Given that c-Myc is a well-recognized downstream effector of the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway and plays a central role in regulating glycolysis, its involvement in LTBP2-mediated metabolic effects is a biologically plausible hypothesis. In our study, we observed that LTBP2 knockdown significantly reduced glucose uptake and lactate production, whereas LTBP2 overexpression enhanced these glycolytic activities in meningioma cells. In line with these findings, LTBP2 knockdown also led to decreased expression of glycolytic markers (PKM2, LDHA, HK2, and GLUT1), while its overexpression upregulated these markers. ese results suggest that LTBP2 promotes glycolysis and contributes to altered glucose metabolism in meningioma cells, potentially facilitating tumor progression.

Mechanistically, LTBP2 has been reported to activate the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway [10], which is a key regulatory axis in cancer metabolism and glycolysis [35,36]. e PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway enhances the transcription and activity of several glycolysis-related enzymes and transporters. erefore, we hypothesize that LTBP2 may exert its pro-glycolytic effects in meningioma cells by activating PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling, which in turn upregulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes metabolic reprogramming. e PI3K/AKT and mTOR/c-Myc pathways are critical networks regulating cellular proliferation and metabolism. PI3K/AKT pathway activation promotes cell proliferation and glycolysis, while AKT-mediated phosphorylation of mTOR further drives protein synthesis and metabolic reprogramming [37]. Zhang L et al. demonstrated that inhibiting the PI3K/AKT pathway in meningioma cells suppresses cell proliferation, inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [38]. Additionally, Pinker B et al. reported that mTOR activation enhances glycolysis, further linking this pathway to tumor development [39]. Given that mTOR activity is regulated by PI3K/AKT signaling and Merlin [40]-a tumor suppressor encoded by the NF2 gene commonly inactivated in meningiomas-preliminary evidence from early-phase clinical trials suggests that targeting mTOR may offer therapeutic benefits in treating drug-resistant meningiomas [41].

c-Myc, a transcription factor regulated by mTOR, plays a key role in regulating cell metabolism and proliferation. It directly increases the levels of genes involved in glycolysis such as GLUT1 and LDHA, leading to increased metabolic activity [42]. As a key oncogene, c-Myc is implicated in various brain tumors, with studies by Ashrafizadeh M et al. demonstrating its potential as a therapeutic target in brain cancers, including meningiomas [43]. Although derived from pancreatic cancer, the findings by Ala Mshowing that c-Myc overexpression promotes tumor aggressiveness, aerobic glycolysis, and chemotherapy resistance-highlight the conserved role of c-Myc-mediated metabolic reprogramming across different tumor types, thereby supporting its relevance in meningioma pathogenesis as well [44]. Given these insights, and based on prior evidence suggesting a link between LTBP2 and oncogenic signaling pathways, we hypothesized that LTBP2 might contribute to metabolic reprogramming in meningiomas. is investigation demonstrated support that LTBP2 regulates glycolysis by activating the PI3K/ AKT and mTOR/c-Myc pathways in meningioma cells. LTBP2 overexpression enhanced glycolytic activity, cell invasion, migration, and proliferation while preventing apoptosis. Conversely, knockdown of c-Myc attenuated the LTBP2-induced enhancement of glycolysis, invasion, migration, and proliferation, and partially restored apoptosis, bringing these cellular phenotypes closer to control levels. ese findings suggest that LTBP2mediated tumor progression is regulated by c-Myc activity. ese conclusions are supported by Western blot analyses of pathway-related proteins and functional assays including glycolysis measurements and cell behavior assessments. While these findings underscore the potential central role of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR/c-Myc axis in meningioma progression, further studies are needed to fully validate these mechanisms. Targeting LTBP2 or its downstream pathways may help suppress tumor growth and inhibit the glycolytic reprogramming associated with aggressive tumor behavior.

One limitation of this study is the lack of validation of LTBP2 expression in clinical meningioma tissue samples. Additionally, the correlation between c-MYC and LTBP2 mRNA expression remains inconclusive. In the GSE84263 dataset, a weak negative correlation was observed (p = 0.03, r = 0.19), whereas our experimental results showed both to be upregulated in meningioma cells, suggesting a positive correlation. ese discrepancies may arise from sample specificity, biological differences, or technical variations. Due to limited tissue availability, we were unable to confirm LTBP2 expression at the tissue level. Future studies will focus on collecting patient-derived specimens to validate these findings, expanding the sample size, and further investigating the clinical relevance of LTBP2 in meningioma through multi-platform verification and in vitro and in vivo studies.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In conclusion, this investigation shows the crucial function of LTBP2 in the malignant progression of meningiomas. Our findings indicate that LTBP2 is significantly overexpressed in meningioma cells, promoting cell migration, invasion, and proliferation while inhibiting apoptosis.

e regulatory impacts of LTBP2 on glycolysis were confirmed through alterations in lactate production and glucose uptake, linked to the levels of important glycolytic proteins. Notably, LTBP2 activates the PI3K/AKT and mTOR/c-Myc signaling pathways, hereby promoting the aggressive behavior of meningioma cells.

e interplay between LTBP2 and c-Myc was particularly critical, as c-Myc knockdown partially reversed the effects of LTBP2 overexpression. ese insights highlight LTBP2 as a potential therapeutic target, emphasizing the need for further investigation into its mechanisms in meningioma pathology.
